subject: Civil Engineering
title: Site Investigation for Tunnels
description: A quick, practical guide to Site Investigation for Tunnels.

hook.text: You can't see underground — but you must know every layer before you start digging.

buildup.text: Boreholes drill cylindrical samples — revealing soil layers, rock quality, and water levels.

discovery.text: Geophysical methods — seismic reflection, ground-penetrating radar — map hidden features.

twist.text: A single undetected fault zone can flood a tunnel or collapse the face — surprises are costly.

climax.text: The Channel Tunnel drilled 4,000 boreholes from ships before committing to the route.

punchline.text: Tunnel success starts above ground — with knowing what's below before you dig.

quiz.question: Why did the Channel Tunnel project drill 4,000 boreholes before construction?
options: They needed to drain all groundwater from the tunnel route first
Thorough investigation of ground conditions was essential to avoid costly surprises
The boreholes served as pilot tunnels for the final alignment

details.summary: Site investigation for tunnels maps geological conditions along the alignment using boreholes, geophysical surveys, groundwater measurements, and laboratory testing.
details.whyItMatters: Ground conditions determine every aspect of tunnel design and construction. Insufficient investigation has caused some of the most expensive project failures in civil engineering history.
takeaways: Boreholes along the alignment sample rock and soil at regular intervals
Geophysical methods map conditions between boreholes without direct sampling
Groundwater pressure is often the most critical parameter for tunnel stability

faq.question: Why is site investigation so critical for tunnel projects?
faq.answer: Unlike surface structures where foundations can be adjusted during construction, tunnels must pass through whatever ground exists along the alignment. Unexpected conditions like water-bearing fault zones, weak soil pockets, or contaminated ground can halt construction.

faq.question: What geophysical methods supplement borehole investigations?
faq.answer: Seismic refraction and reflection map rock surface depth and quality. Ground-penetrating radar detects cavities and utilities. Electrical resistivity identifies groundwater zones. These methods fill gaps between boreholes but cannot fully replace direct sampling of the ground.
